claims.text: The target material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
Superconductivity in the target alloy is controlled by its average electron–phonon coupling strength.
The average electron–phonon coupling strength is modulated by local lattice distortions arising from the balance between titanium and heavy transition metals.
Changing the titanium-to-heavy-transition-metal ratio induces changes in local lattice distortion.
Differences in atomic size and electronic configuration among titanium and heavy transition metals induce subtle short-range ordering.
Altering the balance between titanium and heavy transition metals shifts the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Altering the balance between titanium and heavy transition metals changes electron–phonon coupling strength.
Composition-induced lattice distortions enhance or suppress the pairing interactions required for superconductivity.
Increasing the relative heavy-transition-metal content while preserving a single-phase solid solution enhances electron–phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron–phonon coupling should be observable through phonon softening or related measurements.
Increasing the relative heavy-transition-metal content increases the superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline composition.
The baseline composition has a lower superconducting transition temperature than the proposed heavy-transition-metal-enriched compositions.
Electron–phonon interactions dominate under the proposed cryogenic superconductivity-testing conditions.
The proposed relationship may cease to apply when significant structural ordering or phase separation occurs.
